composite function: A function f(g(x)) where g is applied first and its output becomes the input of f.
domain: The set of all input x-values for which a function is defined.
domain of composite: The x-values where x is in g's domain and g(x) is in f's domain.
even function: A function satisfying f(−x) = f(x), with a graph symmetric about the y-axis.
function: A rule assigning to each input x exactly one output y.
function operations: Combining functions by adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing their outputs.
graph of inverse: The graph of f⁻¹, obtained by reflecting the graph of f across the line y = x.
horizontal line test: A graph represents a one-to-one function if every horizontal line meets it at most once.
horizontal shift: The transformation y = f(x − h), moving the graph right for h > 0 and left for h < 0.
horizontal stretch/compression: The transformation y = f(bx), compressing horizontally if |b| > 1 and stretching if 0 < |b| < 1.
increasing interval: An interval where the function's values rise as x moves from left to right.
inner/outer function: In f(g(x)), g is the inner function applied first and f is the outer function applied next.
inverse function: The function f⁻¹ that reverses f, so f(a) = b means f⁻¹(b) = a.
key-point tracking: Graphing transformations by applying them only to a parent function's key points.
local extremum: A point where a function reaches a local maximum or minimum relative to nearby values.
odd function: A function satisfying f(−x) = −f(x), with a graph symmetric about the origin.
one-to-one function: A function where different inputs always give different outputs.
parent function: The simplest basic form of a function family before any transformations are applied.
piecewise function: A function defined by different expressions on different intervals of its domain.
range: The set of all output y-values a function actually produces.
reflection over x-axis: The transformation y = −f(x), flipping the graph across the x-axis.
reflection over y-axis: The transformation y = f(−x), flipping the graph across the y-axis.
vertical shift: The transformation y = f(x) + k, moving the graph up for k > 0 and down for k < 0.
vertical stretch/compression: The transformation y = af(x), stretching vertically if |a| > 1 and compressing if 0 < |a| < 1.
change of base formula: Rewriting a logarithm in a new base: log_b x = log x / log b = ln x / ln b.
crossing an asymptote: A graph can never cross a vertical asymptote but may cross a horizontal or slant one.
definition of logarithm: log_b x = y means b^y = x; the logarithm asks what power of b gives x.
discontinuity: A point where a function is undefined or not continuous, such as a hole or asymptote.
end behavior: How a function's values behave as x approaches positive or negative infinity.
exponential function: A function f(x) = b^x with b > 0, b ≠ 1, increasing if b > 1 and decreasing if 0 < b < 1.
extraneous solution: A solution produced by algebraic steps that fails to satisfy the original equation.
factor theorem: p(c) = 0 if and only if (x − c) is a factor of the polynomial p(x).
hole / removable discontinuity: A single missing point where a common factor cancels from numerator and denominator.
horizontal asymptote: The y-value a rational function approaches as x goes to plus or minus infinity.
logarithmic function: A function f(x) = log_b x, the inverse of the exponential function b^x.
multiplicity: How many times a factor (x − c) repeats; odd multiplicity crosses the x-axis, even touches it.
natural exponential & logarithm: The functions e^x and ln x, based on the constant e ≈ 2.71828.
oblique / slant asymptote: A diagonal asymptote occurring when the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's.
properties of logarithms: Rules: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y, log(xⁿ) = n log x.
rational root theorem: Any rational root p/q of an integer-coefficient polynomial has p dividing the constant and q the leading coefficient.
remainder theorem: The remainder when dividing p(x) by (x − c) equals p(c).
sign analysis: Testing values on each side of an asymptote to determine the sign of the function there.
synthetic division: A shortcut using only coefficients to divide a polynomial by a linear factor (x − c).
vertical asymptote: A vertical line x = c that a graph approaches infinitely as the denominator nears zero.
zero / root: A value x = c where f(c) = 0, corresponding to an x-intercept of the graph.
ambiguous case, ssa: An SSA triangle setup that may yield zero, one, or two valid triangles.
amplitude: The value |A| in A sin(Bx + C) + D, the maximum distance of the graph from its midline.
arc length & sector area: For a sector with radius r and angle θ in radians, arc length is rθ and area is ½r²θ.
cosecant & secant graphs: Reciprocal graphs of sine and cosine, with vertical asymptotes where sine or cosine equals zero.
cotangent graph: The graph of cot x = 1/tan x, with period π and asymptotes where sin x = 0.
coterminal angles: Angles in standard position sharing the same terminal side, differing by multiples of 360° (or 2π).
double-angle formulas: Identities like sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ.
general solution: All solutions of a trig equation, accounting for the function's periodicity.
law of cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem.
law of sines: In any triangle, a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
period: The horizontal length of one complete cycle of a periodic function; 2π/|B| for sin(Bx).
phase shift: The horizontal shift of a sinusoid, equal to −C/B in A sin(Bx + C).
pythagorean identity: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, derived from the unit circle.
quarter points: The five points dividing one period of a sine or cosine graph into four equal parts.
radian: The central angle that subtends an arc equal in length to the radius; 2π radians is one full turn.
reference angle: The positive acute angle between a terminal side and the x-axis.
special angle values: The exact trig values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°.
sum/difference formulas: Identities expressing sin(A ± B) and cos(A ± B) in terms of sines and cosines of A and B.
tangent graph: The graph of tan x = sin x / cos x, with period π and asymptotes where cos x = 0.
unit circle: The circle x² + y² = 1, where a terminal side meets it at the point (cos θ, sin θ).
arithmetic sequence: A sequence with a constant difference d between consecutive terms; aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
arithmetic series partial sum: The sum of n arithmetic terms: Sₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ).
binomial theorem: An expansion of (a + b)ⁿ as a sum of terms C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ.
continuity: A function is continuous at a if f(a) exists, its limit exists there, and the two are equal.
direct substitution: Evaluating a limit by plugging x = a directly into a continuous function.
factorial, n!: The product n × (n−1) × … × 1, with 0! defined as 1.
geometric sequence: A sequence with a constant ratio r between consecutive terms; aₙ = a₁·rⁿ⁻¹.
geometric series partial sum: The sum of n geometric terms: Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.
identifying type: Checking whether a sequence has a constant difference (arithmetic) or ratio (geometric).
indeterminate form 0/0: A limit form requiring algebra, such as factoring or conjugates, since direct substitution gives 0/0.
infinite discontinuity: A point where f(x) tends to ±∞, appearing as a vertical asymptote.
infinite geometric series: The sum a₁/(1 − r) of an infinite geometric series, convergent only when |r| < 1.
jump discontinuity: A point where the left and right limits both exist but differ.
limit: The value f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a, whether or not f(a) exists.
one-sided limits: The values a function approaches from the left (x→a⁻) or the right (x→a⁺) of a point.
pascal's triangle: A triangular array of binomial coefficients, each entry the sum of the two above it.
removable discontinuity: A point where the limit exists but the function value is missing or different, shown as a hole.
sigma notation, σ: A compact way to write a sum, Σ from k = m to n of aₖ.
sum properties: Identities such as the binomial coefficients of row n summing to 2ⁿ.
symmetry of binomial coefficients: The identity C(n, k) = C(n, n−k).
